cards.prompt: Convert the category column to pandas' category dtype to save memory. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: category dtype stores each distinct value once and uses small integer codes for the rest — a big memory win for text columns with few distinct values repeated many times.
cards.whenToUse: A text column with a small number of repeating values (like region, status, or category) in a large DataFrame.
cards.commonMistake: Applying category dtype to a column that's almost all unique values (like an id or a free-text field) — there's little to no memory benefit there.
cards.example:
# 0    Shoes
# 1    Shoes
# dtype: category
# Categories (2, object): ['Bags', 'Shoes']

cards.prompt: Check exactly how much memory each column of df is using, including the true size of text columns. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Without deep=True, object columns report only the pointer size, not the actual string data — deep=True walks the real objects for an accurate number.
cards.whenToUse: Diagnosing which columns are actually driving a DataFrame's memory footprint before optimizing.
cards.commonMistake: Comparing memory_usage() (shallow) across a DataFrame with text columns — it drastically understates their real size.
cards.example:
# Index         132
# region        420
# category      410
# revenue        64
# units          64
# dtype: int64

cards.prompt: Downcast the revenue column to the smallest integer dtype that can still hold its values. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: downcast='integer' shrinks a column from the default int64 to the smallest int subtype (int8/16/32) that fits every value, without changing what the numbers mean.
cards.whenToUse: Large DataFrames with numeric columns whose values comfortably fit in a smaller type than pandas' int64 default.
cards.commonMistake: Downcasting a column that might later hold larger values (e.g. after a join or an update) — the smaller dtype can silently overflow or need re-casting.
cards.example: # same values, dtype shrinks from int64 to int8

cards.prompt: Set units to 0 for every row where revenue is over 100, in a single loc call rather than two chained bracket operations. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: A single loc call assigns directly into df; chaining df[df['revenue'] > 100]['units'] = 0 instead assigns into a temporary copy that's immediately discarded, and often triggers a SettingWithCopyWarning.
cards.whenToUse: Any conditional assignment back into a DataFrame — this is the reliable pattern, not a bracket-then-bracket chain.
cards.commonMistake: Writing df[condition]['column'] = value — it may appear to work, may warn, or may silently do nothing, depending on pandas internals.
cards.example: # rows where revenue > 100 now have units == 0

cards.prompt: List every row of df as lightweight namedtuples, a faster alternative to iterrows() for row-by-row iteration. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: itertuples() returns namedtuples instead of rebuilding a Series per row (what iterrows() does), which is significantly faster on large DataFrames.
cards.whenToUse: Row-by-row iteration is genuinely unavoidable and no vectorized alternative exists.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for either iterrows() or itertuples() by default — vectorized operations (column-wise math, .apply(), boolean masks) are almost always faster than any row-by-row loop.

cards.prompt: Filter df for rows where revenue is over 60 and units is over 5, using query() instead of chained boolean indexing. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: query() parses the expression and evaluates it with numexpr under the hood when available, which can outperform boolean indexing on large DataFrames — and it reads more like plain English.
cards.whenToUse: Filters with several conditions, on large DataFrames, where readability and (sometimes) speed both matter.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming query() is always faster — for small DataFrames the overhead of parsing the expression can make it slower than a direct boolean mask.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 5   East    Shoes       70      7

cards.prompt: Count how many rows have revenue over 100, without building a filtered copy of df just to call len() on it.
cards.why: A boolean Series sums to a count directly (True counts as 1) — no need to materialize a filtered DataFrame first just to measure its length.
cards.whenToUse: You only need the count of matching rows, not the matching rows themselves.
cards.commonMistake: Writing len(df[df['revenue'] > 100]) — correct, but it builds an entire filtered DataFrame just to throw it away after counting.

cards.prompt: Build a boolean mask for rows where region is 'West' or 'East', without chaining multiple == comparisons with |. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: isin() checks membership against a list in one call — a chain of == comparisons joined by | does the same thing but scales worse to read and to write as the list of options grows.
cards.whenToUse: Filtering against a set of allowed values, especially as that set grows past 2-3 options.
cards.commonMistake: Writing df['region'] == ['West', 'East'] directly — that's not valid membership testing, it's a shape-mismatched comparison.

cards.prompt: Which is the fastest way to add a 10% markup to every value in the revenue column?
cards.why: Plain arithmetic on a Series runs as a single vectorized, compiled operation across every element — apply() and map() both fall back to calling a Python function once per row, which is much slower at scale.
cards.whenToUse: Any time the transformation is expressible as ordinary arithmetic or a built-in vectorized method — reach for apply()/map() only when it genuinely isn't.
cards.commonMistake: Defaulting to .apply(lambda x: ...) out of habit even when the same result is available as plain vectorized arithmetic.

cards.prompt: Sort df by revenue descending, assigning the result rather than relying on inplace=True. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Despite the name, inplace=True doesn't skip creating a new internal array in most pandas operations — it just hides the reassignment step, with no real memory or speed advantage, and it breaks method chaining.
cards.whenToUse: Any pandas transformation — prefer reassigning the result (df = df.sort_values(...)) over inplace=True as the default habit.
cards.commonMistake: Choosing inplace=True believing it's the 'faster' or 'more memory-efficient' option — internally it's still building a new result, just assigning it back to the same name.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9

cards.prompt: Sum units per region using groupby, instead of manually looping over each distinct region. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: groupby() computes per-group aggregation in vectorized, compiled code — a manual Python loop over unique regions, filtering and summing each one, does the same work far slower.
cards.whenToUse: Any per-category aggregation — sum, mean, count — reach for groupby() before writing a manual loop.
cards.commonMistake: Looping over df['region'].unique() and filtering df for each one — it recomputes a full scan of df once per category instead of a single grouped pass.
cards.example:
# region
# East     22
# North    11
# West     25
# Name: units, dtype: int64

cards.prompt: Filter df to rows where category contains the text 'Shoe', using a vectorized string method instead of apply(). Fill in the blank.
cards.why: The .str accessor runs string operations across the whole Series in one vectorized call — apply(lambda x: 'Shoe' in x) does the same check, just one slow Python function call per row.
cards.whenToUse: Any text-matching filter on a column — substring search, prefix/suffix checks, case changes.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for .apply() with a lambda for string logic that .str already covers directly and faster.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12
# 1   East    Shoes       95      9

cards.prompt: Load csv_path with revenue as a smaller int32 dtype from the start, instead of loading as int64 and downcasting afterward. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: Specifying dtype at load time avoids ever allocating the larger default dtype in the first place — cheaper than loading big and downcasting after.
cards.whenToUse: Loading a large CSV where you already know a column's values fit comfortably in a smaller numeric type.
cards.commonMistake: Loading with default dtypes and downcasting afterward as a matter of habit — fine occasionally, but wasteful for consistently large files where the smaller dtype is known upfront.
cards.example: # revenue column loads directly as int32 instead of int64
